summary: Describes how GIST can use SCTP and DTLS for connection mode operation, where it currently uses TCP or TLS over TCP. It is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: GIST is the layer that carries setup messages for the Next Steps in Signalling protocol family. It normally runs over TCP, and this RFC offers an alternative built on SCTP. SCTP keeps messages separate in its own streams, can use several network addresses so a broken link does not end the connection, and can be told to give up on a message that has been waiting too long. DTLS is then used to protect the traffic.

subtitle: How the signalling transport GIST can run over SCTP, and how DTLS secures it.

tldr.problem: GIST, the transport used by the Next Steps in Signalling protocol family, runs over TCP, which cannot drop a stale message, blocks other sessions behind one lost message, and has no way to survive a path failure.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds two new choices to GIST: SCTP as the underlying transport, with its multiple streams, multihoming and partial reliability, and DTLS as the security mechanism that protects the resulting messaging associations.
tldr.outcome: It is an Experimental document that registers MA-Protocol-ID 3 for Forwards-SCTP and 4 for DTLS. It has since been updated by RFC 8996, which deprecates TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1.

facts.label: MA-Protocol-Options field
facts.value: 4 bytes: a 16-bit SCTP port number and 16 reserved bits

facts.label: MA-protocol-options in a Response
facts.value: 2-byte port number followed by 2 pad bytes

facts.label: Connection direction
facts.value: Forwards, from the querying node towards the responder

facts.label: Minimum DTLS version
facts.value: DTLS v1.0; the highest version both peers support must be used

today: RFC 6084 was published in January 2011 as an Experimental document, published for examination and experimental implementation. It has since been updated by RFC 8996, which deprecates TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1.

sections.title: Why GIST Needs Another Transport
sections.content:
GIST, the General Internet Signaling Transport, is specified for connection mode operation on top of a byte-stream-oriented transport protocol that provides reliable, in-sequence delivery, which in practice means TCP.

The RFC gives three reasons to look elsewhere. Some Next Steps in Signaling (NSIS) Signaling Layer Protocol context information has a definite lifetime, so the GIST transport could benefit from flexible retransmission, allowing stale messages that are held up by congestion to be dropped. Together with the head-of-line blocking and multihoming problems of TCP, these considerations argue that GIST implementations should support SCTP as an optional transport protocol.

Like TCP, SCTP supports reliability, congestion control and fragmentation. Unlike TCP, it offers several things that suit signalling: multiple streams, multiple IP addresses for path failure recovery, and message-oriented transport, so the framing that a byte stream would need is built in. Its Partial Reliability extension, PR-SCTP, supports partial retransmission based on a programmable retransmission timer. DTLS, in turn, provides a workable way to secure SCTP, which lets SCTP use almost all of its transport features and extensions.

Using GIST over SCTP requires no change to the high-level operation and structure of GIST. It does need extra interface code and configuration support, so that applications can use the extra transport features when appropriate. An SCTP implementation used to transport GIST MUST support the optional feature of fragmentation of SCTP user messages.
sections.plainLanguage: TCP is a single ordered pipe of bytes, so one lost message holds up everything behind it and there is no second address to fall back on. SCTP is built for signalling instead: it keeps sessions apart, it can hold several network addresses, and it can be told to stop retrying a message that no longer matters.

sections.title: Opening a Messaging Association over SCTP
sections.content:
The base GIST specification allows two protocols in a messaging association, Forwards-TCP and TLS. This RFC adds a third, Forwards-SCTP, with the value 3. Support for it is OPTIONAL. If the protocol is offered, the MA-protocol-options data must also be carried in the Stack Configuration Data object: in a query the field carries no information apart from its header, and in a response it carries a 2-byte port number at which the connection will be accepted, followed by 2 pad bytes.

The connection is opened in the forwards direction, from the querying node towards the responder, the same as Forwards-TCP. The querying node may use any source address and source port. The destination must be derived from the response: the address comes from the interface-address in the Network-Layer-Information object and the port comes from the Stack Configuration Data object as described above.

Associations using Forwards-SCTP can carry messages with the transfer attribute Reliable=True. If an error occurs on the SCTP connection, such as a reset, which the SCTP socket API can report, GIST must report it to the NSLPs. In the multihoming case, when the destination address of a GIST-over-SCTP peer changes, the SCTP API notifies GIST about the availability of different SCTP endpoint addresses and about a possible change of the primary path.
sections.plainLanguage: The new option works like the existing TCP one: the node asking the question opens the connection towards the node that will answer. The answer tells the first node which port to connect to, and the first node then opens the connection there.

sections.title: Streams, Partial Reliability and Path Recovery
sections.content:
SCTP defines unidirectional streams, and this document uses the idea of a bidirectional stream. Implementations MUST establish both the downstream and the upstream unidirectional SCTP streams and use the same stream identifier in both directions, so that the two form one bidirectional stream.

Because SCTP supports multiple streams, different resources, such as different NSLP sessions, can use different streams instead of being kept in step along one connection as TCP requires. There are limits to that. All GIST messages for a particular session MUST be sent over the same SCTP stream, so that the NSLP assumption of in-order delivery still holds. Multiple sessions MAY share the same stream, depending on local policy. The GIST concept of messaging association reuse is not affected by any of this, and all the rules in the GIST specification remain valid.

PR-SCTP adds a timed reliability service, in which the user states per message how persistent the transport service should be in trying to deliver it. Because SCTP bundles chunks, reliable and partially reliable messages can be multiplexed over a single PR-SCTP association. An SCTP implementation for GIST SHOULD therefore try to establish a PR-SCTP association using the timed reliability service instead of a standard SCTP association, if one is available. The reason is concrete: with a normally reliable session, if a node has already sent the first transmission before the lifetime expires, the message MUST be sent as a normal reliable message anyway. During congestion that is unfortunate, because the retransmission wastes bandwidth that other, unexpired messages could have used.

Multihoming is a partial answer to path failures, but a limited one. The default Message Routing Method is path-coupled, so if the primary path fails for the SCTP association it most likely fails for the IP traffic being signalled too, and GIST would have to refresh the NSIS nodes to the alternative path anyway. Where the two endpoints of a multihomed SCTP association, but none of the intermediate nodes, support NSIS, GIST over SCTP does give a robust way to deliver NSLP messages when the primary path fails but an alternative path between those endpoints is available. Multihoming also gives GIST and the NSLP a second way to notice a route change, and the alternative path can carry traffic during the time between noticing the change and recovering from it.
sections.plainLanguage: Each session gets its own channel inside the connection, so a lost message in one session does not hold up another. A message can also be given a deadline, after which the transport stops trying to resend it and frees the bandwidth for messages that still matter. With several network addresses on the connection, a broken path can be detected and worked around, though only the two ends of the connection need to support it for that to help.

sections.title: What Changes for the Signalling Application
sections.content:
The GIST specification defines an abstract API between GIST and the NSLPs. This RFC does not change the API itself, but some parameters mean slightly different things over SCTP. Only the primitives that need special consideration are listed.

The first is the Timeout parameter in the API call SendMessage. In the GIST specification it represents the length of time GIST should attempt to send the message before indicating an error. With PR-SCTP, the same parameter is used as the timeout for the timed reliability service.

The second is the NetworkNotification primitive, which is passed from GIST to a signalling application to say that a network event of possible interest to that application has occurred. If SCTP detects a failure of the primary path, GIST SHOULD indicate this event to the NSLP by calling the primitive with the Network-Notification-Type Routing Status Change. The RFC asks for this notification even when SCTP was able to keep the connection open because of its multihoming, since the traffic itself may still have to move to another path.
sections.plainLanguage: The application above GIST keeps using the same two calls it used before. One of them, the send timeout, now doubles as the deadline after which the transport stops retrying a message. The other, the network notification, is used to tell the application that the connection has switched to a different path.

sections.title: The MA-Protocol-Options Field
sections.content:
The MA-protocol-options field is used for SCTP in the Stack-Configuration-Data object of GIST. It is a 32-bit field. The first 16 bits carry the SCTP port number, which is the port at which the responder will accept SCTP connections. The last 16 bits are reserved. The SCTP port number is only supplied when the field is sent by the responder.

No MA-protocol-options field is required for DTLS. The configuration information for the transport protocol that DTLS runs over, such as the SCTP port number, is provided by the MA-protocol-options field of that protocol.

IANA has registered two new codepoints in the MA-Protocol-ID registry created by the GIST specification: value 3 for SCTP opened in the forwards direction, and value 4 for DTLS initiated in the forwards direction. The RFC notes that the DTLS value is never used on its own but is always coupled with a transport protocol given in the stack proposal.
sections.plainLanguage: Only one thing has to be carried over the signalling channel to set up the SCTP option: the port number on which the responder will take connections. It is a 32-bit field, and the second half of it is reserved and unused.

sections.title: Securing GIST with DTLS
sections.content:
The RFC adds a second MA-Protocol-ID, DTLS with the value 4, for the use of DTLS in GIST. It denotes basic use of datagram transport layer channel security, initially in conjunction with GIST over SCTP. It provides server, meaning GIST transport receiver, authentication and integrity, as long as the NULL ciphersuite is not selected during ciphersuite negotiation, and optionally replay protection for control packets. Securing GIST over SCTP with DTLS lets GIST take advantage of the features SCTP provides, and it works the same way as TLS for GIST in the base specification, with a stack proposal that carries both the SCTP and the DTLS MA-Protocol-IDs during the GIST handshake phase.

Use of DTLS for securing GIST over datagram transport protocols MUST be implemented and SHOULD be used. Implementations MUST NOT negotiate protocol versions prior to DTLS v1.0 and MUST use the highest protocol version supported by both peers. NULL authentication and integrity ciphers MUST NOT be negotiated for GIST nodes that support DTLS; the NULL ciphersuites may be used for confidentiality ciphers. The same rules for negotiating TLS ciphersuites as in the GIST specification apply. Because DTLS renegotiation can change the connection security parameters without the application knowing, renegotiation is RECOMMENDED to be disabled for GIST over DTLS.

The security considerations of the GIST, SCTP and DTLS specifications apply. The RFC adds one point: although DTLS over SCTP does not support replay detection, the SCTP replay protection mechanisms should be able to protect NSIS messages transported over GIST over DTLS over SCTP from replay attacks. The RFC also notes that it defines no NAT traversal procedures for GIST over SCTP, though an approach for SCTP NAT traversal is described elsewhere.
sections.plainLanguage: The security layer is DTLS, the datagram version of TLS. It must be used when the transport underneath is a datagram one, old DTLS versions are not allowed, and the null choices that would provide no real protection are ruled out for authentication and integrity. Renegotiation is better switched off, because it can change the protection without telling the application.

viz.caption: WHY SCTP INSTEAD OF TCP FOR SIGNALLING

cells: Byte stream, so framing must be provided separately
One dropped message can hold up other sessions on the same connection
Avoided by putting different sessions on different streams
No alternative address to fall back on
Multiple IP addresses for path failure recovery
Always retries until the message is delivered
Fully reliable, or partially reliable with a timed reliability service

fields.desc: Port number at which the responder will accept SCTP connections. Only supplied if sent by the responder.
